title: FA/49/2023 of BEENA MEHRA Vs POORAN SINGH MEHRA

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
SRI JUSTICE VIPIN SANGHI, C.J.
AND
SRI JUSTICE RAKESH THAPLIYAL, J.
11th JULY, 2023
FIRST APPEAL No. 49 OF 2023
Smt. Beena Mehra ...........Appellant
Versus
Pooran Singh Mehra ..........Respondent
Counsel for the appellant : Mr. Sanjay Bhatt.
Counsel for the respondent : None.

Upon hearing the learned Counsel, the Court
made the following
JUDGMENT : (per Sri Rakesh Thapliyal, J.)
 By the present Appeal, the appellant is
challenging the judgment and decree dated
20/28.02.2023 passed by the learned Judge, Family
Court, Almora in Marriage Dissolution Case No. 37 of
2020 Pooran Singh Mehra vs. Smt. Beena Mehra,
whereby a decree of divorce was sought on the ground
of cruelty, as provided under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as
'the Act').

2
2. According to the respondent, who was the
plaintiff in the Suit filed before the Family Judge,
Almora, the marriage of the appellant and the
respondent had been solemnized on 12.06.2005 at
Village Thapla, Post Ganiyadholi, Tehsil Ranikhet,
District Almora according to Hindu rites and customs.
Out of their wedlock, two children, namely Taruna
Mehra and Tushar Mehra, were born, who are presently
living with the plaintiff. For a few years, the relationship
in between the appellant-wife and the respondent-husband was good. The respondent also got fashion
designing course, beautician course, and make-up
artist course done to the appellant. The respondent got
a beauty-parlour started for the appellant at
Bhajanpura at Delhi. After the opening of the beauty-parlour, the behavior of the appellant started getting
changed towards the respondent. She started finding
occasions to fight with the respondent on everything,
due to which the respondent got worried, as all his
earnings he had put in that shop for the appellant so
that the family of the respondent could be economically
firm and the children may study well. The respondent
used to do some other job, and he handed-over the
responsibility of the children and the beauty-parlour to

3
the appellant. According to the respondent, the
appellant misused the liberty given to her, and she
started having physical relations with other people.
On 28.02.2020, the appellant fled away with one Sanju
Chauhan. A missing report of his wife (appellant) was
got lodged by the respondent on 02.03.2020 at Police
Station Khajurikhas, North East Delhi, as by
28.02.2020, he kept searching for his wife at all the
probable places and inquired about her from her
brothers at her maternal home and her brother-in-law
(Jeeja) at Jaipur. When the respondent inquired from
Deepak Rawat, the brother of his wife about his wife on
28.02.2020 on phone, he clearly stated that if you
come to our house, we will shoot you. According to the
respondent, prior to fleeing away, the behavior of the
appellant towards the respondent had become
indifferent; no physical relations were kept with him
since then; she keeps physical relationship with one
other person, namely Sanju Chauhan and is involved in
adultery. According to the respondent, the appellant
had herself given a letter in her own handwriting to the
appellant on 02.06.2019 admitting therein her
relationship with Vishal Chaudhary Panwar, to which
her sister and brothers were witnesses, and she had

4
also given a letter in writing on 28.02.2020 showing
her unwillingness to live with the respondent, and she
stated therein to have left the house of the respondent
on her own. On these grounds, the respondent prayed
before the Judge, Family Court, Almora that the
marriage solemnized on 12.06.2005 in between the
parties be dissolved by passing a decree of divorce.
4. By filing her Written Statement Paper No.
20A, the appellant rebutted the plaint. Therein, she
admitted her marriage with the appellant to have been
solemnized on 12.06.2005 at Village Thapla according
to Hindu rites and customs, and two children having
been born out of their wedlock on 25.09.2006 and
30.07.2009 respectively. She further stated therein
that Misc. Criminal Case No. 02/2006 titled as "Beena
Mehra vs. Pooran Singh Mehra and others" under
Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic
Violence Act, 2005 is pending between the parties
before the Court of Judicial Magistrate, Ranikhet. After
one year of the marriage, when the appellant gave
birth to a girl child on 25.09.2006, the respondent and
his mother Smt. Haruli Devi beaten-up and abused the
appellant. The appellant was abused for giving birth to
a girl child, due to which the respondent would take the

5
appellant to Delhi for three-four months sometimes. In
2008, the appellant again got pregnant, but because of
being beaten-up by the respondent after getting drunk,
miscarriage of her five-month pregnancy took place,
due to which the appellant became physically and
mentally weak. On 30.07.2009, the appellant gave
birth to a boy, after which the appellant started living
at Delhi with the respondent and her children. It has
been stated by the appellant that she learnt the work of
sewing machine and beauty-parlour in Delhi, so that
she may earn something for her own expenditure, but
when she started the work of beauty-parlour in Delhi,
then the respondent, by coming to her workplace in
drunken condition, used to abuse her and raise
allegations on her character. After the birth of two
children, the respondent became habitual of beating-up
the appellant, abusing her and making derogatory
remarks on her character in which Lal Singh Mehra-the
elder brother-in-law (Jeth), Dhana Mehra-elder sister-in-law (Jethani), Arjun Singh Pindari-brother-in-law
(Nandoi), Saraswati Pindari-sister-in-law (Nanand)
used to provide their assistance by instigating him. The
mother-in-law of the appellant used to instigate the
respondent on phone against the appellant. In order to

6
save her marital life, the appellant kept on bearing the
physical, mental, economical and gender related
harassment caused by the appellant and his relatives.
The appellant had to shut the work of the beauty-parlour down due to the abnormal behavior of the
respondent, and the beauty-parlour shop of the
appellant was sold-off by the respondent. Even after
selling the beauty-parlour shop, the respondent kept on
doing character assassination, mental and physical
torture by doubting her every act. By extending threat
to kill the children, the respondent used to ask the
appellant to bring money from her maternal house,
which demand was fulfilled by the appellant by the time
her father was alive. It is stated by the appellant that
after the death of her father, the financial position of
the maternal house became very bad, due to which it
was not possible for the appellant to fulfill the demand
of money of the respondent. Because of this reason,
domestic violence by the respondent against the
appellant started increasing. On 27.02.2020, the
appellant and his relatives, by beating-up the appellant
and by getting written against the own character of the
appellant, got her signatures on a paper and by
threatening her in the morning on 28.02.2020 got her

7
boarded in a Bus for Haldwani at Anand Vihar Bus
Stand. Thereafter, the appellant reached the house of
her elder sister at Rudrapur at about 11 p.m. on
28.02.2020 and informed her about the incident
happened with her. After that, information about this
was also given by to her brother and mother living at
Jaipur. On the next day, i.e. on 29.02.2020, the elder
sister of the appellant took the appellant to Brij Lal
Hospital and Research Centre, Nainital Road, Haldwani
and got her medical treatment done.
5. According to the appellant, she came to know
about a fake missing report being lodged by the
respondent against her after she received a phone call
from Police Station Khajurikhas, and came to know
from summons received from the Family Court that the
respondent had filed a case under Section 12 of the
Act. The appellant narrated the entire incident to the
SHO, Police Station Khajurikhas by giving an
application and getting her statement recorded. It is
stated by the appellant that by leveling false and wrong
allegations against her, the suit for divorce was filed by
the respondent. She further stated that she still
wanted to live with the respondent and her children.
She further stated that the father of the appellant also

8
gave about Rs. one lac fifty thousand in addition to
earrings, gold nose-ring, gold tops, articles etc. as gift
in the marriage, according to his capacity. She,
thereafter, prayed that the plaint of the respondent
filed against the appellant be rejected with costs.
6. In support of their cases, both the parties adduced
their respective documentary and oral evidence. The
respondent got examined himself as PW-1, and his son,
namely Tushar Mehra as PW-2, whereas the appellant
got examined herself as DW-1.
7. After hearing the arguments advanced by learned
counsel for both the parties and considering the
evidence adduced by both the parties, learned Judge,
Family Court, Almora vide judgment and decree dated
20/28.02.2023 allowed the petition filed by the
respondent-Pooran Singh Mehra under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Act against the appellant-Smt. Beena Mehra,
granted a decree of divorce and dissolved the marriage
of the parties solemnized on 12.06.2005.
8. Aggrieved by the said judgment, the present First
Appeal has been preferred by the appellant (wife)
under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, read
with Section 19 of the Family Courts Act 1984, praying
that the present First Appeal be allowed by setting

9
aside the impugned judgment and decree dated
20/28.02.2023 passed by Judge, Family Court, Almora
in Marriage Dissolution Petition No. 37 of 2020 be set
aside.
9. Learned counsel for the appellant submits
that the judgment passed by the Family Court cannot
sustain, as the same has been passed without
appreciating the evidence of the parties. He,
thereafter, argues that the petition was filed on the
ground that the appellant (wife) was living in adultery
with some other man, who was not her husband, but
the said person was not even arrayed as a party-respondent in the petition, and as such, the petition
should have been dismissed on this ground alone. He
further argues that the adultery was not even proved
by the respondent (husband). It is also argued by
counsel for the appellant that the decree of divorce had
been sought on the ground of adultery, but the divorce
was granted on the ground of cruelty, which was not
even pleaded and proved by admissible evidence, and
as such, the judgment passed by the Family Court
cannot sustain. It is further argued that there are
contradictions in the statements of PW-1 and PW-2,
and the appellant denied the illicit relationship.

10
ANALYSIS:
10. The appellant (wife) has challenged the
impugned judgment and decree primarily on the
following two grounds:-
(i) The impugned judgment has been passed on
the ground of 'cruelty', though the respondent
(husband) had filed the suit of divorce on the
ground of 'adultery'.
(ii) For establishing 'cruelty' on the ground of
which the impugned judgment has been passed,
no evidence was produced by the respondent
(husband).
11. For determining the first issue, it is settled
principle of law that the concept of mental cruelty
cannot remain static. It is bound to change with the
passage of time, impact of modern culture through
print and electronic media and value system, etc. etc.
What may be mental cruelty now may not remain a
mental cruelty after a passage of time or vice versa.
There can never be any straitjacket formula or fixed
parameters for determining mental cruelty in
matrimonial matters. The prudent and appropriate way
to adjudicate the case would be to evaluate it on its

11
peculiar facts and circumstances while taking aforesaid
factors in consideration. The Supreme Court in the
case of Samar Ghosh vs. Jaya Ghosh (2007) 4 SCC
511 laid down certain guiding factors giving some
illustrations / instances of human behavior, though
they are not exhaustive, which may be relevant in
dealing with the cases of "mental cruelty". The
instances, as elaborated by the Supreme Court in the
aforesaid judgment, are as follows:-
"No uniform standard can ever be laid down
for guidance, yet we deem it appropriate to
enumerate some instances of human behaviour
which may be relevant in dealing with the cases of
'mental cruelty'. The instances indicated in the
succeeding paragraphs are only illustrative and
not exhaustive.
(i) On consideration of complete matrimonial life
of the parties, acute mental pain, agony and
suffering as would not make possible for the
parties to live with each other could come within
the broad parameters of mental cruelty.
(ii) On comprehensive appraisal of the entire
matrimonial life of the parties, it becomes
abundantly clear that situation is such that the
wronged party cannot reasonably be asked to put
up with such conduct and continue to live with
other party.
(iii) Mere coldness or lack of affection cannot
amount to cruelty, frequent rudeness of language,
petulance of manner, indifference and neglect may
reach such a degree that it makes the married life
for the other spouse absolutely intolerable.
(iv) Mental cruelty is a state of mind. The feeling
of deep anguish, disappointment, frustration in
one spouse caused by the conduct of other for a
long time may lead to mental cruelty.

12
(v) A sustained course of abusive and humiliating
treatment calculated to torture, discommode or
render miserable life of the spouse.
(vi) Sustained unjustifiable conduct and behaviour
of one spouse actually affecting physical and
mental health of the other spouse. The treatment
complained of and the resultant danger or
apprehension must be very grave, substantial and
weighty.
(vii) Sustained reprehensible conduct, studied
neglect, indifference or total departure from the
normal standard of conjugal kindness causing
injury to mental health or deriving sadistic
pleasure can also amount to mental cruelty.
(viii) The conduct must be much more than
jealousy, selfishness, possessiveness, which
causes unhappiness and dissatisfaction and
emotional upset may not be a ground for grant of
divorce on the ground of mental cruelty.
(ix) Mere trivial irritations, quarrels, normal wear
and tear of the married life which happens in day
to day life would not be adequate for grant of
divorce on the ground of mental cruelty.
(x) The married life should be reviewed as a whole
and a few isolated instances over a period of years
will not amount to cruelty. The ill-conduct must be
persistent for a fairly lengthy period, where the
relationship has deteriorated to an extent that
because of the acts and behaviour of a spouse,
the wronged party finds it extremely difficult to
live with the other party any longer, may amount
to mental cruelty.
(xi) If a husband submits himself for an operation
of sterilization without medical reasons and
without the consent or knowledge of his wife and
similarly if the wife undergoes vasectomy or
abortion without medical reason or without the
consent or knowledge of her husband, such an act
of the spouse may lead to mental cruelty.
(xii) Unilateral decision of refusal to have
intercourse for considerable period without there
being any physical incapacity or valid reason may
amount to mental cruelty.
(xiii) Unilateral decision of either husband or wife
after marriage not to have child from the marriage
may amount to cruelty.

13
(xiv) Where there has been a long period of
continuous separation, it may fairly be concluded
that the matrimonial bond is beyond repair. The
marriage becomes a fiction though supported by a
legal tie. By refusing to sever that tie, the law in
such cases, does not serve the sanctity of
marriage; on the contrary, it shows scant regard
for the feelings and emotions of the parties. In
such like situations, it may lead to mental
cruelty."
12. Now for determining the issue whether
extra-marital affair, or adultery amounts to 'cruelty',
since the Supreme Court in the aforesaid case observed
that no uniform standard can be laid down for
guidance, however, in the case of K.V. Prakash Babu
v. State of Karnataka (2017) 11 SCC 176, the
Supreme Court has observed, in Paragraph-18, that
extra-marital affairs may not in all circumstances invite
conviction under Section 306 IPC, but definitely that
can be a ground for divorce or other reliefs in a
matrimonial dispute. For ready reference, the relevant
extract of the said judgment is being reproduced as
under:-
"18. Having said that we intend to make it clear
that if the husband gets involved in an extra-marital affair that may not in all circumstances
invite conviction under Section 306 IPC but
definitely that can be a ground for divorce or other
reliefs in a matrimonial dispute under other
enactments. And we so clarify."

14
13. Looking into the facts of the present case in
the light of the judgments of the Supreme Court as
aforesaid, the ground of adultery also falls in the
ground of cruelty. Merely on the basis that the ground
of cruelty does not include adultery, it does not mean
that if any of the party is indulged in extra-marital
affairs, it does not amount to cruelty against the other
party. If we go by the plain consideration of the
illustration / instances, as given by the Supreme Court
in the case of Samar Ghosh (supra), the ground of
adultery cannot be excluded from the scope of cruelty.
A married life depends on the mutual trust of the both
the spouses. However, if that trust falls then
matrimonial life cannot be continued. If one spouse is
indulged in adultery or in any extra-marital affair, then
such spouse loses his / her trust of the other spouse,
and such conduct involving extra-marital affair amounts
to cruelty to other spouse.
14. Apart from this, involvement in extra-marital
affair causes a deep anguish, disappointment, and
frustration, and such a conduct of one spouse amounts
to mental cruelty to the other spouse.
15. Now we come to the next ground for
challenging the impugned judgment. The appellant

15
submits that no evidence has been produced, or
adduced for the purpose of establishing cruelty.
16. In dealing with this ground, we should keep
in mind that 'cruelty' has not been defined in the Act.
 Cruelty can be physical or mental. Cruelty which is a
ground for dissolution of marriage may be defined as
willful and unjustifiable conduct of such character as to
cause danger to life, limb or health, bodily or mental,
or as to give rise to a reasonable apprehension of such
a danger. The question of mental cruelty has to be
considered in the light of the norms of marital ties of
the particular society to which the parties belong, their
social values, status, environment in which they live. If
from the conduct of the spouse same is established
and/or an inference can be legitimately drawn that the
treatment of the spouse is such that it causes an
apprehension in the mind of the other spouse, about
his or her mental welfare then this conduct amounts to
cruelty.
17. The concept, a proof beyond the shadow of
doubt, is to be applied to criminal trials and not to civil
matters and certainly not to matters of such delicate
personal relationship as those of husband and wife.
Therefore, one has to see what are the probabilities in

16
a case and legal cruelty has to be found out, not merely
as a matter of fact, but as the effect on the mind of the
complainant spouse because of the acts or omissions of
the other. Cruelty may be physical or corporeal or may
be mental. In physical cruelty, there can be tangible
and direct evidence, but in the case of mental cruelty
there may not at the same time be direct evidence. In
cases where there is no direct evidence, Courts are
required to probe into the mental process and mental
effect of incidents that are brought out in evidence.
18. The expression "cruelty" in respect of
matrimonial duties and obligations depends on human
conduct or human behaviour. The cruelty may be
mental or physical, intentional or unintentional. If it is
physical, the Court will have no problem in determining
it. It is a question of fact and degree. In other way, if
it is mental, the problem presents difficulties.
19. First, the enquiry must begin as to the nature
of cruel treatment, second the impact of such
treatment in the mind of the spouse, whether it caused
reasonable apprehension that it would be harmful or
injurious to live with the other. Ultimately, it is a matter
of inference to be drawn by taking into account the

17
nature of the conduct and its effect on the complaining
spouse.
20. Now to constitute 'cruelty', the conduct
 complained of should be "grave and weighty" so as to
come to the conclusion that the petitioner spouse
cannot be reasonably expected to live with the other
spouse.
21. So far as the present case is concerned, the
husband had sought divorce on the ground of cruelty,
and as we have observed above, this ground is based
on adultery, and the conduct of the appellant, which we
have already discussed above, falls under the category
of 'mental cruelty', and the Family Court has rightly
decreed the suit for divorce.
22. Apart from this, in the present case, the
Family Court in the impugned judgment held that the
appellant (wife) was engaged in a relationship with
another individual and she expressed her unwillingness
to continue living with the respondent (husband), and
she departed from her husband's house on 28.02.2020
to live with the another person. The Family Court, in
our view, has rightly concluded that the conduct of the
appellant having been engaged in adulterous

18
relationship and deserting the husband and her children
amounts to inflicting mental cruelty upon the husband.
23. In view of the observations as made above,
we do not find any ground, which warrants interference
by this Court in the impugned judgment.
24. Accordingly, the instant Appeal is dismissed,
and the judgment and the decree dated 20/28.02.2023
passed by the learned Judge, Family Court, Almora in
Marriage Dissolution Case No. 37 of 2020 Pooran Singh
Mehra vs. Smt. Beena Mehra, are upheld.
25. No order as to costs.
